1. Core Clinical Tension: A 53-year-old male cattle farmer from Kerala, South India, presents with a three-week history of watery diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, weight loss, non-migratory lower extremity rash, hypokalemia, and leukocytosis without peripheral eosinophilia (2%). His clinical history of diabetes mellitus, alcohol use disorder, and chronic cavitary lung disease treated with anti-tubercular therapy creates a complex host phenotype. The clinical presentation mimics acute bacterial gastroenteritis, Clostridioides difficile colitis, or gastrointestinal malignancy, masking a fatal helminthic hyperinfection syndrome in which intestinal barrier breakdown permits secondary invasive bacterial bloodstream seeding.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission narrative concludes following clinical examination of the pedal edema and lower extremity erythematous rash, baseline hematology showing leukocytosis without eosinophilia, severe hypokalemia (2.6 mEq/L), hyperglycemia (274 mg/dL), negative viral hepatitis/HIV serologies, abdominal ultrasound/CT showing hepatic hypodensities, chest CT showing cavitary lung lesions, and normal upper endoscopy, strictly before stool wet mount microscopy, stool agar culture, and stool/blood bacterial cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute bacterial enteritis is considered when stool cultures grow Aeromonas sobria, but this represents a secondary bacterial colonizer facilitated by helminthic mucosal disruption; Clostridioides difficile colitis is ruled out by negative stool toxin assays; gastrointestinal malignancy with hepatic metastasis is excluded by normal upper endoscopy and benign fatty/inflammatory liver changes; the definitive diagnosis is established by the microscopic demonstration of motile rhabditiform larvae and agar culture trail signs characteristic of Strongyloides stercoralis.
case_prompt:
A 53-year-old male from Kerala, South India, presented to a tertiary hospital with a three-week history of watery, non-bloody loose stools occurring three to four times per day. He reported intermittent vague abdominal pain, decreased appetite, and a 3- to 4-kg weight loss over the preceding month. He denied fever, vomiting, respiratory symptoms, or acute urticaria. His past medical history was significant for alcohol use disorder, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia on regular medications for two years, as well as an ischemic stroke resulting in residual left hemiparesis two years prior. He also had a history of chronic cavitary pulmonary infection treated with multi-drug antimycobacterial therapy for the previous six months. He had no history of intravenous drug use, high-risk sexual behavior, or recent travel outside the state, and consumed only cooked food. He worked barefoot as a cattle farmer on his farm, which featured a shallow freshwater pond used for fish aquaculture; there was no known open-field defecation in the work area.

On physical examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. He had bilateral pitting pedal edema and a non-migratory macular erythematous rash over the anterior aspect of both lower legs of two weeks' duration. Abdominal and systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Routine laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin level of 9.6 g/dL, an elevated total white blood cell count of 13,600/µL with 90% polymorphonuclear cells, 6% lymphocytes, 2% eosinophils, and 2% monocytes, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 78 mm/h. Serum electrolytes demonstrated marked hypokalemia with a potassium level of 2.6 mEq/L. Random blood glucose at admission was markedly elevated at 274 mg/dL. Screening for human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B surface antigen, and hepatitis C antibodies was negative. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated fatty hepatomegaly with focal hepatic lesions. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed several hypodense lesions in segment 5 of the liver with mild hepatomegaly. Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated bilateral upper lobe cavitary lesions. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed and revealed normal mucosal findings.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute bacterial enteritis / Aeromonas sobria infection
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and leukocytosis led to the isolation of Aeromonas sobria on stool bacteriological culture; however, antibacterial therapy failed to arrest the underlying illness because the bacteria were opportunistic secondary invaders crossing an intestinal mucosa disrupted by nematode hyperinfection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The bacteriological culture of stool yielded Aeromonas sobria, which was sensitive to ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline and cotrimoxazole.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: In a diabetic patient with recent chronic antimicrobial exposure presenting with copious watery diarrhea and leukocytosis, pseudomembranous colitis was a prominent diagnostic consideration, but stool testing for Clostridium difficile toxins was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Stool occult blood (Hemospot kit, standard guaiac method, Tulip Diagnostics, Goa, India) and Clostridium difficile toxin (VIDAS difficile toxin A and B, bioMerieux SA) were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Weight loss, anorexia, chronic diarrhea, and hypodense hepatic lesions on abdominal CT raised high concern for occult gastrointestinal malignancy with metastatic dissemination, but upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal, and the liver lesions reflected fatty/inflammatory changes in the setting of chronic alcohol use and systemic illness.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed, which was normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point was stool wet preparation microscopy, which revealed abundant motile rhabditiform larvae, corroborated by the classic agar culture plate 'positive trail sign' demonstrating bacterial tracks created by crawling larvae, confirming hyperinfection by the soil-transmitted nematode Strongyloides stercoralis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Wet preparation revealed numerous motile larvae in the rhabditiform stage, which measured 100-400 microm in lengthx15-20 microm in width and had a short buccal cavity.

editor_comments: Complies strictly with Stanford MedCaseReasoning guidelines. The case prompt ends before stool microscopy, agar culture, and stool bacterial cultures, containing zero spoilers or parasite/pathogen nomenclature.
